stories.title: Introducing the pkg.go.dev API
stories.snippet: The Go Blog Introducing the pkg.go.dev API Ethan Lee, Hana Kim, and Jonathan Amsterdam 21 May 2026 Since its inception, pkg.go.dev has established itself as the Go community’s primary resource for package documentation and discovery. While we initially prioritized creating a comprehensive and highly accessible web interface for users, the need for programmatic access has become increasingly
stories.summary: Go has launched an official API for pkg.go.dev, providing programmatic access to metadata about published Go modules and addressing the community's need for alternatives to web scraping. The stateless, GET-only service hosts its primary endpoints under the /v1beta path, with the team planning a transition to a formal v1 release following a stability period. Core endpoints cover packages, modules, versions, search, symbols, imported-by relationships, and vulnerabilities. Following a "precision over convenience" design principle, the API requires clients to explicitly specify the module when a package path is ambiguous, rather than automatically applying the "longest module path" rule used by the web interface. The API supports version selection through semver tags or the master and main branch names, which resolve automatically to pseudo-versions. A reference command-line client called pkgsite-cli is available to demonstrate interaction with the API.

stories.title: Type Construction and Cycle Detection
stories.snippet: The Go Blog Type Construction and Cycle Detection Mark Freeman 24 March 2026 Go’s static typing is an important part of why Go is a good fit for production systems that have to be robust and reliable. When a Go package is compiled, it is first parsed—meaning that the Go source code within that package is converted into an abstract syntax tree (or AST). This AST is then passed to the Go type
stories.summary: Go's type checker constructs internal representations for each type as it traverses the abstract syntax tree, with types transitioning from "under construction" to "complete" once their dependencies are resolved. Type construction follows a depth-first process, and recursive types like `type T []U` with `type U *T` can result in incomplete types during evaluation, since they reference themselves before construction finishes. The type checker handles this by deferring checks that require deconstruction until all types are complete, since type construction itself doesn't need to examine internals. However, certain cases like `type T [unsafe.Sizeof(T{})]int` create problems because calculating the array's size requires deconstruction, leading to a cycle where neither type can complete. This is addressed through cycle detection, which identifies such invalid cyclic definitions while still allowing operations on incomplete values that don't require deconstruction.

stories.title: //go:fix inline and the source-level inliner
stories.snippet: The Go Blog //go:fix inline and the source-level inliner Alan Donovan 10 March 2026 .beforeafter { justify-content: center; display: grid; gap: 1em; margin: 1em; grid-template-columns: minmax(min-content, 1fr) auto minmax(min-content, 1fr); font-size: 180%; @media screen and (max-width: 57.7rem) { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } } #content .beforeafter pre { margin: 0em; /* Handled by grid gap */ }
stories.summary: Go 1.26 introduces a source-level inliner as part of the redesigned go fix subcommand, enabling automatic migration of API calls by replacing each call with a copy of the called function's body. Package authors can opt functions into this transformation by adding a //go:fix inline directive, allowing any package to express simple deprecation migrations such as redirecting ioutil.ReadFile to os.ReadFile or correcting parameter ordering in a hypothetical oldmath package. The same inliner powers gopls refactorings like "Inline call," "Change signature," and "Remove unused parameter," and it also works on type aliases and constants. One key challenge is parameter elimination, where the tool tries to substitute arguments for parameters when literals appear, but must be conservative to avoid duplicating magic values. The inliner is about 7,000 lines of dense, compiler-like logic to handle these subtleties correctly.

stories.title: Enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker on nightly
stories.snippet: TL;DR We are enabling the next iteration of the borrow checker (coined Polonius Alpha) on nightly in preparation for stabilization in the next few months. Whaaaaaat? Yes! You heard it right! The next iteration of the Rust borrow checker is coming! Rust's first borrow checker ("AST borrowck") was very limited and was phased out in 2019 in favor of NLL, other than a "migrate mode" that was used to p
stories.summary: The next iteration of Rust's borrow checker, dubbed Polonius Alpha, is being enabled on nightly for testing, with stabilization planned before the end of the year. It enables flow-sensitive borrow checking of lifetime outlives relationships, allowing code that NLL incorrectly rejects to compile correctly. However, Polonius Alpha is not a strict superset of legacy Polonius, as some programs accepted by the original implementation fail to compile under the new formulation. Performance is generally acceptable, though testing on the top 10,000 crates by downloads on crates.io revealed relatively few significant regressions, with the worst case being a 2-3x slowdown. Users who encounter issues can disable Polonius Alpha using the `-Zpolonius=off` flag or in their `.cargo/config.toml` file. Over the coming months, the team will monitor reported issues, address performance regressions, and prepare internal documentation prior to stabilization.

stories.title: Announcing Rust 1.97.1
stories.snippet: The Rust team has published a new point release of Rust, 1.97.1. Rust is a programming language that is empowering everyone to build reliable and efficient software. If you have a previous version of Rust installed via rustup, getting Rust 1.97.1 is as easy as: rustup update stable If you don't have it already, you can get rustup from the appropriate page on our website. What's in 1.97.1 Rust 1.97
stories.summary: Rust 1.97.1 is a new point release of the Rust programming language, which can be obtained by running `rustup update stable` on systems with rustup installed. The release addresses a miscompilation in an LLVM optimization, with the Rust team backporting both an LLVM fix and a disable of the underlying IR change introduced in Rust 1.97.0 that increased the likelihood of the issue occurring. Notably, the underlying miscompilation has existed since at least Rust 1.87. The team encourages users to test future releases by switching to the beta or nightly channel using rustup and to report any bugs encountered. This release reflects the collaborative effort of many contributors in the Rust community.

stories.title: Surgical WAM: A World-Action Model for Data-Efficient Surgical Robot Learning
stories.summary: Learning reliable surgical manipulation policies is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled teleoperated demonstrations, while endoscopic video is comparatively abundant. The authors introduce the Surgical World-Action Model (Surgical WAM), a unified generative model built on Cosmos Policy that jointly predicts future endoscopic observations and executable surgical robot action chunks. Surgical WAM first learns surgical visual dynamics from action-free video and is then fine-tuned on a fixed action-labeled budget, acting as a closed-loop, receding-horizon controller that executes short action prefixes and replans from new observations. On a suite of four simulated surgical manipulation tasks, video pretraining improved the average success rate from 63.5% to 77.8%, including a 20 percentage point gain on PegTransfer. The largest improvements occurred on contact-rich and bimanual tasks, demonstrating that action-free video provides transferable visual dynamics priors for data-efficient surgical robot learning.

stories.title: ConVAWG: A Retrieval-Grounded Framework for Controlled Synthetic Dialogue Generation in Violence Against Women and Girls
stories.summary: ConVAWG is a retrieval-grounded framework designed to generate synthetic multi-turn dialogues depicting Violence Against Women and Girls (VAWG) scenarios, addressing the gap left by limited access to real conversational data due to privacy and legal constraints. The framework moves beyond sentence-level toxicity modeling by constructing scenarios from persona seeds, UK Office for National Statistics demographic patterns, official crime definitions, and retrieved Domestic Homicide Review cases. These scenarios are converted into hierarchical event timelines, from which multi-scene role-play dialogues are generated with targeted activation-steered toxicity control applied to appropriate utterances. The authors release over 6,000 multi-turn dialogue events across 200 scenarios, accompanied by rich scenario-, event-, and turn-level metadata. Evaluation through human assessment, LLM-as-Judge, ablations, and downstream tasks demonstrates strong dialogue quality and domain fidelity.

stories.title: Long-Horizon AI Research for Grothendieck Constant: A Case Study in Human-AI Mathematical Collaboration
stories.summary: Researchers presented a case study exploring how AI agents can be effectively used in mathematics research, specifically to improve bounds on the Grothendieck constant (K_G), a value that captures the hardness gap between combinatorial problems and their continuous relaxations. While the exact value of K_G remains unknown, the team tightened the best known bounds to 6π/11 ≤ K_G ≤ π/(2log(1+√2)) - 10^(-4). These improvements were achieved through an AI research system that produced insights which domain experts deemed novel. The paper provides a detailed account of the authors' experience using AI for mathematical research, discussing the system's strengths and weaknesses. Additionally, they share observations about creating ideal conditions that enabled the AI to arrive at breakthrough insights on this long-horizon research problem.

stories.title: Test-Time Self-Evolving GUI Visual Grounding via Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation
stories.summary: The paper introduces a Test-Time Self-Evolving framework for GUI visual grounding, enabling models to improve after deployment without human-annotated ground truth. The approach establishes a closed-loop of Exploration, Evaluation, Reflection, and Internalization, where an agent predicts grounding coordinates for unseen interfaces and an MLLM-based Reflector assesses the results to provide reasoning reflections. To internalize this knowledge into model weights, the authors propose Reflection-Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation, which translates high-level reasoning into dense token-level supervision through a conditioned self-teacher. A Contrastive Calibration method is also introduced to prevent incorrect auto-regressive prefixes from corrupting supervisory signals during failed explorations. Experiments across six benchmarks demonstrate an average accuracy improvement of 7.4% over the base model, marking the first successful exploitation of on-policy self-distillation for test-time adaptation in this domain.

stories.title: How to Verify Consistency of Probabilistic Claims
stories.summary: This paper addresses whether a probabilistic predictor's answers to many conditional-probability queries can be verified for self-consistency in polynomial time. The authors construct an interactive PCP where a model is specified by a probability circuit P and a confidence circuit Q, and a polynomial-time verifier can check approximate consistency by evaluating the circuits at only a few points while interacting with an untrusted prover via a witnessing distribution. For explicit probabilistic claims of the form Pr[Y=1|X=x]=p over n Boolean variables, they place l_2-approximate consistency in NP with certificates of length O(mn+log B), showing that a small additive gap removes dependence on bit-precision B. The work has implications for AI safety, where honest probabilistic predictions about unwanted outcomes from AI actions are critical, and provides a complexity-theoretic foundation for certifying predictor self-consistency. It also represents an initial step toward training predictive models to prove their own consistency.

stories.title: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.snippet: Npm-scan: Modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem
stories.summary: npm-scan is a supply chain security tool designed for the npm ecosystem, hosted on GitHub by lateos-ai. It claims to detect threats that other security tools like npm audit, Snyk, and Socket miss, including obfuscated payloads, credential stealers, kernel rootkits, eBPF hooks, memory extraction, GitHub spoofing, and AI-targeted attacks. The project is available as an npm package (@lateos/npm-scan) and ships with over 830 passing tests, dual-licensed under MIT or BLA. Its repository contains 225 commits and includes a CLI, backend, API, Helm chart for Kubernetes deployment, and a GitHub Action for integration into CI/CD workflows. The main branch is at commit 78425141 and the project advertises itself as "modern supply chain security for the npm ecosystem."

stories.title: Show HN: Open-Source Greptile Alternative
stories.summary: Juror is an open-source GitHub Action from Juror-AI that uses frontier models in parallel to review pull requests, positioning itself as an alternative to Greptile. The repository has gained 82 stars and 9 forks across 48 commits, with directories for benchmarks, docs, scripts, source code, and tests. A bundled benchmark on a production pull request claims Juror Fast identified 4 out of 6 P0–P2 defects at 100% precision, compared to Greptile's 1 out of 6 at 50% precision, though the project acknowledges this is a single-PR seed rather than a statistically sufficient benchmark. The project is MIT licensed, requires Node version 20 or higher, and practices dogfooding by using Juror to review its own code through a dedicated workflow.

stories.title: How Tailscale helped find the SQLite WAL-Reset bug
stories.snippet: Previously, the SQLite release fixing this bug. Comments
stories.summary: Tailscale experienced 19 separate instances of SQLite database corruption over six months, disrupting their control plane service that manages mesh network metadata for customers. Although corruption affected only a fraction of tailnets, recovery required halting the control plane process on affected shards, preventing new devices from connecting and blocking access to the admin console. After extensive investigation failed to identify a trigger, Tailscale engaged SQLite's developers for professional support and built a transaction logging pipeline to aid restoration. This pipeline revealed that committed data was inexplicably invisible to subsequent transactions, pointing toward the Write-Ahead Logging checkpoint process. Working with SQLite's core developers, Tailscale ultimately helped uncover and fix a 16-year-old bug deep within SQLite's checkpoint mechanism.

stories.title: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813
stories.summary: DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 is a large-scale mixture-of-experts model from DeepSeek, released as the GA version of DeepSeek V4 Pro on August 12, 2026. It supports text input and output with a context window of 1,048,576 tokens. Pricing is set at $0.435 per million input tokens and $0.87 per million output tokens, with a cache read rate of $0.003625 per million tokens. On OpenRouter, the model is hosted by a single provider, with requests forwarded directly without routing decisions.

stories.title: I hate packaging my software for Linux
stories.summary: The author of Fresh encountered significant challenges packaging their software for Linux due to the fragmented ecosystem, trying numerous distribution channels including npm, cargo, AppImage, Flatpak, deb, rpm, AUR, nix, mise, homebrew for Linux, and Gentoo GURU. Each method presented drawbacks: npm raised security concerns, Flatpak's sandboxing conflicted with the terminal-based TUI, AppImage suffered slow startup times due to FUSE-mounting, and deb/rpm packages lacked automatic updates since they weren't accepted into official repositories. Additional complications included Debian's requirement to package all Rust dependencies, AUR's read-only status following security breaches, and mise breaking unexpectedly due to a GitHub certificate rotation. Moving forward, the author plans to focus on a statically linked musl binary with a built-in self-updating mechanism as the primary release channel for Linux, hoping to reduce the maintenance burden of supporting multiple distribution methods.
